```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", echo = FALSE)
library(pfmatch)
v <- pf_variants
fmt <- function(x) formatC(x, big.mark = ",", format = "d")
pct <- function(a, b) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * a / b)
tab <- function(d, ...) knitr::kable(d, format = "html", row.names = FALSE, ...)
# knitr::kable is the only rendering dependency; everything below is computed
# from the bundled pf_variants, so this vignette needs no reference, no corpus
# and no cascade run.
```

How recipient names and addresses actually vary in the 990-PF filings, which
of those variations the pipeline already absorbs, and which ones decide whether
a grant resolves to an EIN.

Everything here is computed from `pf_variants`: `r fmt(nrow(v))` pairs of
recipient renderings filed at the same street and ZIP, across
`r fmt(length(unique(v$group_id)))` addresses. In each pair the cascade
resolved one rendering (`YES`) and returned `MAYBE` on the other. They come
from the 50,000-case triangulation run over population
`` `r attr(v, "population")` ``.

## Read this first: these pairs survived normalization

The pairs are not a random sample of variation. They are the residue.

Before any pass runs, `npmatch::np_normalize()` has already uppercased, dropped
a leading `THE`, rewritten `&` as `AND`, expanded `FDN` to `FOUNDATION` and
contracted USPS street suffixes; `pf_dedup()` has then collapsed renderings
sharing an identity key into a single recipient. So a pair that differs *only*
in a way the pipeline handles never reaches the comparator as two things and
never appears here.

What that buys: the table is a regression corpus. Every row is a live case that
reached the comparator and split. Tighten the normalizer and specific rows
should move; the rows recorded as already closed should stay closed.

What it costs: `pf_variants` tells you nothing about variation the normalizer
already fixes. For that, compare the `*_differs` columns (the filed text)
against the `*_key_equal` columns (what the normalizer made of it).

```{r survived}
d <- data.frame(
  check = c("ZIP5 agrees inside the pair",
            "filed street text differs",
            "...but the normalized street key agrees",
            "normalized name keys agree anyway",
            "blocking intact (ZIP5 and state both usable)"),
  pairs = fmt(c(sum(v$zip5_equal), sum(v$street_differs),
                sum(v$street_differs & v$street_key_equal),
                sum(v$name_key_equal), sum(v$blocking_intact))),
  share = c(pct(sum(v$zip5_equal), nrow(v)), pct(sum(v$street_differs), nrow(v)),
            pct(sum(v$street_differs & v$street_key_equal), sum(v$street_differs)),
            pct(sum(v$name_key_equal), nrow(v)),
            pct(sum(v$blocking_intact), nrow(v))),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
tab(d, col.names = c("", "pairs", "share"))
```

ZIP5 agrees in every pair because the group is *defined* by street-plus-ZIP5,
which is also why this table cannot be used to study ZIP variation.

## It is not ground truth

The triangulation verdicts are silver, `confidence = "low"`, and
unadjudicated. Writing the anchor's EIN onto every other rendering at the
address is the assumption under test, not a fact.

So `expected_same_org` is `TRUE` on `r sum(!is.na(v$expected_same_org))` rows —
where the two names are the same string under a documented cosmetic
transformation at an identical address — and `NA`, never `FALSE`, on the other
`r fmt(sum(is.na(v$expected_same_org)))`. Two examples of why a string test
cannot decide it:

- `US OLYMPIC AND PARALYMPIC FOUNDATION` and `USOC` share no tokens and are
  the same family of organization.
- `MARINE CORPS UNIVERSITY FOUNDATION` and `MARINE CORP SCHOLARSHIP FUND`
  share a distinctive token and are two different charities.

`label_basis` records which rows are waiting for a human.

## Name variants

```{r name-classes}
nc <- as.data.frame(table(v$name_class), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
names(nc) <- c("name_class", "pairs")
nc <- nc[order(-nc$pairs), ]
nc$share <- pct(nc$pairs, nrow(v))
nc$med_lev <- round(tapply(v$name_lev, v$name_class, median)[nc$name_class], 1)
nc$med_jaccard <- round(tapply(v$name_jaccard, v$name_class, median)[nc$name_class], 2)
nc$key_agrees <- tapply(v$name_key_equal, v$name_class, sum)[nc$name_class]
nc$pairs <- fmt(nc$pairs)
tab(nc, col.names = c("class", "pairs", "share", "median edit distance",
                      "median token Jaccard", "name keys agree"))
```

The cosmetic classes everyone expects to dominate are almost absent, and that
is the normalizer working: it has already closed them upstream. What is left is
dominated by names that are genuinely different strings.

`name keys agree` is the column to watch. Where it is non-zero the normalizer
*did* close the name difference and the two renderings still reached the
comparator separately — covered in "A seam" below.

### Exemplars

Six per class, from the `curated` subset.

```{r name-examples, results = "asis"}
ord <- names(sort(table(v$name_class), decreasing = TRUE))
for (k in ord) {
  s <- v[v$curated & v$name_class == k, ]
  if (!nrow(s)) next
  s <- s[order(-s$a_score), ][seq_len(min(4L, nrow(s))), ]
  cat("\n**", k, "**\n\n", sep = "")
  print(tab(data.frame(
    `resolved (YES)` = s$a_name, `unresolved (MAYBE)` = s$b_name,
    `name key agrees` = s$name_key_equal, `edit dist` = s$name_lev,
    jaccard = s$name_jaccard, `YES score` = round(s$a_score, 3),
    `MAYBE score` = ifelse(is.na(s$b_score), "-", sprintf("%.3f", s$b_score)),
    check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)))
  cat("\n")
}
```

## Address variants

```{r addr-classes}
ac <- as.data.frame(table(v$addr_class), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
names(ac) <- c("addr_class", "pairs")
ac <- ac[order(-ac$pairs), ]
ac$share <- pct(ac$pairs, nrow(v))
ac$blocking_intact <- pct(tapply(v$blocking_intact, v$addr_class, sum)[ac$addr_class],
                          table(v$addr_class)[ac$addr_class])
ac$pairs <- fmt(ac$pairs)
tab(ac, col.names = c("class", "pairs", "share", "blocking still intact"))
```

### There is no address score

Worth stating plainly, because it is the single most common wrong assumption
about this pipeline. `pf_staged_passes()` blocks on `name_key` or `dba_key`
crossed with `zip5` or `state`, and nothing else:

```{r passes}
p <- pf_staged_passes("lean", concat = TRUE)
tab(data.frame(
  pass = vapply(p, function(x) x$name, ""),
  criteria = vapply(p, function(x) x$desc, ""),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
```

`street`, `unit` and `city` are carried through `pf_map_grants()` and
normalized into `street_key`, but **no pass reads them**. The address is a
blocking constraint, never a score. Consequences:

- A city spelling difference — `FT LAUDERDALE` against `Fort Lauderdale` —
  cannot change the outcome. There are `r fmt(sum(v$city_differs))` such pairs
  here and blocking stays intact in every one of them.
- A suite line cannot separate two organizations in one building, however
  carefully it is filed.
- The one address field that *can* break a match is the **state**, which blocks
  stages A2–A5 and all of stage B. It disagrees in
  `r sum(v$state_differs)` pairs, and the disagreements are adjacent-letter
  filing errors:

```{r state}
s <- v[v$state_differs, c("a_name", "a_state", "b_name", "b_state")]
s <- s[seq_len(min(6L, nrow(s))), ]
tab(s, col.names = c("resolved (YES)", "state", "unresolved (MAYBE)", "state"))
```

Since ZIP5 is present and agrees in every one of these pairs, a ZIP5-to-state
repair would fix them outright.

### Where street normalization does pay

Not inside a group — by construction every pair already keyed to the same
street. It pays in *forming* groups at all. The filed street text differs in
`r fmt(sum(v$street_differs))` pairs here, and the normalizer reconciles
`r sum(v$street_differs & v$street_key_equal)` of them:

```{r street}
s <- v[v$street_differs & v$street_key_equal,
       c("a_street", "b_street", "a_street_key")]
s <- unique(s)[seq_len(min(6L, nrow(unique(s)))), ]
tab(s, col.names = c("filed (YES side)", "filed (MAYBE side)", "normalized key"))
```

A missing space before `SUITE`, `Street` against `ST`, `ROAD` against `RD`.
Measured over the whole corpus rather than these pairs, normalizing the street
collapses 528,862 of 2,326,459 distinct address keys — 22.7% — and brings
58,815 addresses above the two-rendering threshold that are currently split
across spellings and so form no group at all.

The caution: a normalizer that drops the secondary-unit designator to achieve
that will also merge `STE 100` with `STE 200`, which are different tenants.
Distinct units are rare at these addresses, so the trade is probably worth
making, but it is a trade.

## What decides YES against MAYBE

```{r pass-strength}
k <- v[!is.na(v$a_score) & !is.na(v$b_score), ]
tab(data.frame(
  side = c("resolved (YES)", "unresolved (MAYBE)"),
  `median score` = round(c(median(k$a_score), median(k$b_score)), 3),
  `exact name+ZIP5` = c(pct(sum(k$a_pass == "A1-name-zip5"), nrow(k)),
                        pct(sum(k$b_pass == "A1-name-zip5"), nrow(k))),
  `token-blocked` = c(pct(sum(grepl("^B", k$a_pass)), nrow(k)),
                      pct(sum(grepl("^B", k$b_pass)), nrow(k))),
  check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
```

### A seam: identity is keyed on one thing, blocking on another

`pf_dedup()` keys identity on `name_full` — deliberately, so that an
organization is not merged with its affiliate by a `name_key` that has already
thrown the affiliate suffix away. The cascade then blocks stage A1 on
`name_key` crossed with `zip5`. The two disagree, and
`r sum(v$name_key_equal)` pairs land in the gap: same normalized name key,
same street key, same ZIP5, two identities, two different tiers.

```{r seam}
s <- v[v$name_key_equal, c("a_name", "b_name", "a_name_key", "a_score", "b_score")]
s <- s[order(-s$a_score), ][seq_len(min(6L, nrow(s))), ]
s$a_score <- round(s$a_score, 3); s$b_score <- round(s$b_score, 3)
tab(s, col.names = c("resolved (YES)", "unresolved (MAYBE)", "shared name key",
                     "YES score", "MAYBE score"))
```

### When the unresolved side has the better match

The most useful flag in the table. Triangulation writes the anchor's EIN onto
the candidate as `correct_ein`. On `r fmt(sum(v$b_outscores_a))` pairs
(`r pct(sum(v$b_outscores_a), nrow(v))`) the candidate's own match was
*better* than the anchor's — a higher score, or an exact name-plus-ZIP5 hit
against a token-blocked one. On those the silver label runs against the
system's own evidence.

```{r outscore}
s <- v[v$b_outscores_a & !is.na(v$b_score), ]
s <- s[order(s$a_pass_rank - s$b_pass_rank, -s$b_score), ]
s <- s[seq_len(min(8L, nrow(s))), ]
tab(data.frame(
  `anchor (YES)` = s$a_name, `score` = round(s$a_score, 3), pass = s$a_pass,
  `candidate (MAYBE)` = s$b_name, ` score` = round(s$b_score, 3), ` pass` = s$b_pass,
  check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
```

`BETHEL COLLEGE` against `BETHEL UNIVERSITY` is the shape to recognise: a
renamed organization, where the rendering being labelled wrong found the better
reference row. Filter on `b_outscores_a` before trusting a triangulated label.

## Using this as a regression corpus

The pairs carry both the raw filed strings and the keys `np_normalize()` made
of them, so the keys can be recomputed and compared. `tests/testthat/test-variants.R`
does exactly that, in two layers:

- **Invariants** that must hold under any sane normalizer: a leading `THE` never
  decides a name key; streets differing only by suffix spelling or a missing
  space normalize together; streets recorded as genuinely different stay
  different; a city difference never breaks blocking.
- **A pinned check** that every recorded key still reproduces, scoped to the
  `np_normalize_signature()` the fixture was built under
  (`` `r attr(v, "normalizer")` ``). It skips when the normalizer moves, because
  an intentional improvement *should* move keys — and the skip message tells you
  to rebuild with `data-raw/make-pf-variants.R`.

To test a change, re-run the fixture build against the new normalizer and diff
the class table: cosmetic classes should shrink, `name_key_equal` should grow,
and no pair should move from a different-street class into an agreeing one
unless you meant it to.
